Determine prognosis using a validated clinical prediction rule such as the PSI, CRB-65 (best for primary care) or CURB-65. B

Sputum and blood culture, as well as legionella and pneumococcal antigen testing, are recommended for selected patients, particularly those with severe pneumonia and those being treated empirically for MRSA or pseudomonas aeruginosa. C

See for detailed recommendations regarding antibiotic choice. Treat previously healthy outpatients with amoxicillin, doxycycline, or (if resistance <25%) a macrolide. For outpatients with comorbidities use (amoxiclav or a cephalosporin) plus (macrolide or doxycycline), OR a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Treat for at least 5 days and until the patient has been clinically stable and afebrile for 48 to 72 hours.A

For inpatients with nonsevere CAP and no risk factors for MRSA or P. aeruginosa, use combination therapy with a beta-lactam plus a macrolide or doxycycline, OR monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone. For inpatients with severe CAP and no risk factors for MRSA or P. aeruginosa, use a beta-lactam plus macrolide OR beta-lactam plus respiratory fluroquinolone. A

Assess all patients for vaccine status upon treatment for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP); administer vaccines during outpatient treatment or at hospital discharge, if necessary and available. C

background.definition: CAP is commonly defined as an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma that is associated with at least some symptoms of acute infection, accompanied by the presence of an acute infiltrate on CXR or auscultatory findings consistent with pneumonia, in a non-hospitalized patient or a patient who is diagnosed within 48 hours of hospitalization.

list.listitem: Pneumonia is present in 3% to 5% of healthy outpatients presenting with acute respiratory illness.
Pneumonia is diagnosed in 8 to 15/1000 persons per year (4 million adults per year in the United States).
Pneumonia is the eighth leading cause of death in the United States.
Approximately 20% of patients with pneumonia are admitted to the hospital.
Pneumonia occurs when a particularly virulent organism or large inoculum of a pathogen penetrates the pulmonary defense mechanisms and establishes infection within the lung parenchyma.

The defense mechanisms and immune response to an infection can be impaired by many causes, including age, pulmonary disease, anatomic changes, alteration in consciousness, immunosuppressive medications, tobacco use, and other comorbid illnesses.
Inflammatory cells are drawn to the infected area of the lung and release proteolytic enzymes, alter the respiratory epithelium and clearance mechanisms, and cause sputum production.

The pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) should be administered to all children younger than 2 years old. Patients who did not received PCV13 as a child should have shared decision making with their clinician if they should get PCV13 at age 65. However, adults in a high risk group (chronic diseases, immunocompromised, group living, prior pneumonia, substance use, or medications that increase pneumonia risk) should receive the vaccine.B

Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) should be given to all patients older than 65 years and others at a younger age with selected high-risk concurrent diseases including COPD and smokers. BIn high risk patients that need PCV13 and PPSV23, PCV13 is administered first, followed by PPSV23 a year later.

A Cochrane review found that the NNT's to prevent one episode of community acquired pneumonia (CAP) and an acute COPD exacerbation were 19 (95% Cl 13 to 52) and 8 (95% Cl 5 to 58) respectively in COPD patients who received the pneumococcal vaccine.B
Among nursing home patients, use of pneumonia vaccine decreased the rate of pneumonia over 26 months from 20.6% of the patients in the placebo group to 12.5% of the vaccinated group (NNT = 12).B

A Cochrane review found no evidence that pneumococcal vaccination during pregnancy reduces the risk of neonatal infection. However, the overall quality of evidence and number of patients in trials is low.
Influenza vaccine should be considered for all patients older than 50 years, others at risk for influenza complications, household contacts of at-risk persons, and health care workers. A
A randomized trial found no evidence that giving prophylactic antibiotics to hospitalized stroke patients prevents pneumonia in patients with dysphagia.

Consider RSV vaccine for adults 60 years and older. The likelihood of any RSV infection was significantly lower in the vaccine group (0.13% vs 0.34%; number needed to treat [NNT] = 472), as was RSV infection with 2 or more symptoms (0.065% vs 0.19%; NNT = 773) and RSV infection with 3 or more symptoms (0.012% vs 0.082%; NNT = 1416). B
Consider pneumonia in patients with cough, dyspnea, or sputum production, especially if accompanied by fever, altered breath sounds, or rales. C
Perform a CXR to confirm the diagnosis of pneumonia. C

Lung ultrasound is increasingly available, especially in the inpatient and emergency department setting. A systematic review of 16 studies with 2359 participants found an area under the ROC curve of 0.93 (excellent discrimination), a positive LR of 6.0, and a negative LR of 0.12.B
Routine diagnostic tests are optional for outpatients since most do well with empiric antibiotic treatment. C

Sputum and blood culture, as well as legionella and pneumococcal antigen testing, are recommended primarily for patients with severe CAP and those being treated empirically for MRSA or pseudomonas, or in the event of a legionella outbreak. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Wheezing prominent; absence of infectious signs (fever, leukocytosis)
Examination consistent with volume overload; absence of infectious signs
CXR suggests mass lesion, especially in smokers; weight loss common
History of altered mental status or neurologic disease; right middle/lower lobe common

list.listitem: Consider pneumonia in patients with cough, dyspnea, or sputum production, especially if accompanied by fever, altered breath sounds, or rales.

Fever, chills, abnormal vital signs, abnormal lung examination,and leukocytosis all increase the likelihood of pneumonia. Most factors are relatively insensitive and are not good for ruling out pneumonia when absent.

In a study of 1819 ED patients with cough, asymmetric breath sounds, egophony, and increased fremitus best increased the likelihood of CAP in adults when present. A physician judgment that the patient does not have CAP was best at ruling out (LR- 0.2).
Misdiagnosis is relatively common. One study of 48 Michigan hospitals found that 12% of older patients diagnosed and hospitalized with CAP actually did not meet the criteria for diagnosis.

A systematic review concluded that CAP is very unlikely in patients presenting with LRTI symptoms who have HR <100, RR ≤20, temperature ≤101F/38.3C, and normal lung exam (LR 0.10). Given an overall risk of CAP in patients with LRTI of 4%, the risk in patients with normal vitals and lung exam is only 0.4%.

Global physician judgment is a good predictor that an adult patient does or does not have pneumonia with a positive likelihood ratio 7.7 and negative likelihood ratio 0.54. It was less accurate in children (LR+ 2.7, LR- 0.63).

Signs and symptoms are less useful in children younger than 5 years. Most useful in this age range for diagnosing pneumonia are respiratory rate >50 breaths per minute, grunting respirations, chest retractions, and nasal flaring. Absence of fever and RR <40 are helpful for reducing the likelihood of pneumonia. The presence of chest pain is also helpful to diagnose pneumonia in this age group.
Children who appear well, have an oxygen saturation above 94%, and are not tachypneic based on age specific norms are very unlikely to have pneumonia.

See below for Clinical Decision Rules for diagnosis and prognosis. Although the diagnostic rules may not be accurate enough by themselves to guide treatment, they can help guide the physician considering empiric therapy and can confirm clinical judgment regarding the need for CXR.

Perform a CXR to confirm the diagnosis of pneumonia in any patient with acute RTI and at least one of the following abnormal vital signs: temperature higher than 100°F/37.8°C, heart rate greater than 100 bpm, respiratory rate greater than 20 breaths/min; and in any patient with at least two of the following clinical findings: decreased breath sounds, crackles/rales, and absence of asthma.

In contrast, a CXR for a community-dwelling patient is only recommended by the 2009 British Thoracic Society guideline on the management of CAP if the diagnosis is in doubt, progress is not evident during treatment for suspected CAP or the patient is at risk for underlying lung pathology. A CXR is recommended for hospitalized patients.

In infants and children, one study suggested that the combination of a negative CXR in a patient with low clinical suspicion for pneumonia almost excludes the diagnosis of pneumonia and makes it safe to observe without antibiotic therapy.

Pulse oximetry may be useful to identify patients with pneumonia lacking obvious signs and symptoms and to gauge severity. Other diagnostic tests are optional for outpatients since most do well with empiric antibiotic treatment.

The WBC, sedimentation rate, and CRP are only modestly predictive of pneumonia. The British Thoracic Society recommends obtaining a basic metabolic profile as part of the severity assessment and to calculate the CURB-65 (the CRB-65 does not require BUN and is similarly accurate). C-reactive protein (to aid diagnosis and as a baseline), a CBC and liver function for hospitalized patients with CAP.

A meta-analysis in 2020 reviewed the available data on biomarkers and found CRP as the most useful and accurate biomarker for diagnosing CAP. Procalcitonin was found to have a good positive likelihood ratio, but a minimally useful negative likelihood ratio. Leukocytosis has only modest accuracy (LR+ = 3.15). A second meta-analysis found 25 studies with 2864 children and concluded that procalcitonin was of limited value, with LR+ 2.3 and LR- 0.50.

Procalcitonin levels greater than 0.5 mcg/L support a bacterial cause of RTI, whereas a value less than 0.1 mcg/L makes it unlikely that the patient will benefit from antibiotics. A study found that in patients with dyspnea presenting to the ED, when the pretest probability was 13%, a negative procalcitonin lowered the likelihood of pneumonia to 4%. Another study concluded that a procalcitonin of ≥0.25 ng/mL was a valuable predictor for pneumonia in patients with pulmonary infiltrates on CXR. However, procalcitonin-guided use of antibiotics for treatment of suspected lower respiratory tract infection in patients presenting to the ED versus usual care did not decrease antibiotic use. As a result, the 2019 IDSA guidelines do not recommend using procalcitonin to determine the need for antibiotics.

The 2019 IDSA guidelines recommend obtaining sputum and blood cultures in all patients with severe disease and in any patient being treated empirically for MRSA or pseudomonas aeruginosa. They recommend testing for legionella or pneumococcal antigen only with severe CAP or during an outbreak of legionella, and testing for influenza when it is circulating in the community.

Pretreatment blood cultures are positive in only 5% to 14% of patients in one study, hence the recommendation to primarily check them in patients with severe CAP. However, others have questioned the value of blood cultures even in those patients and the American College of Emergency Physicians recommends against routine blood cultures for patients admitted with CAP who are not immunocompromised or have significant comorbidities. In one study of 1743 patients with CAP at 10 hospitals, blood cultures prompted a change of therapy in only 2%, and this change was likely to benefit the patient in only 0.4%. Factors that predict bacteremia in the hospitalized elderly include comorbid liver disease, abnormal vitals, and prior use of antibiotics; these have been gathered in a clinical rule.
Blood cultures are rarely positive in children hospitalized with pneumonia.

A meta-analysis found that approximately 3% of hospitalized patients (outside of a legionella outbreak) with CAP have legionella as the causative organism. Predictors of legionella pneumonia include hyponatremia, elevated LDH, and elevated CRP. A simple score can help identify patients at higher and lower risk of legionella pneumonia. Diarrhea and elevated CK are associated with legionella, but these are too inaccurate to guide therapy.
In ICU patients with hospital or ventilator acquired pneumonia, PCR pathogen testing had a higher sensitivity than conventional culture-based testing.
There are limited data regarding the effects of rapid viral diagnosis of acute RTI in children. A trend was seen toward reduced antibiotic prescribing with testing.

Bedside point-of-care ultrasound can be used to diagnosis pneumonia. A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis found that in patients 0 to 21 years, lung ultrasound was 94% sensitive and 93% specific in diagnosing pneumonia. Another pediatric study found ultrasound to be superior to chest radiograph in sensitivity with similar specificity. A 2017 meta-analysis of adults with pneumonia found that sensitivity and specificity were 88% and 86% respectively for diagnosis pneumonia with an area under the ROC curve of 0.95.
Ultrasound is now endorsed for diagnosis of CAP by updated IDSA/ATS guidelines.
In a small primary care study, POC ultrasound by primary care physicians had LR+ 2.1 and LR- of 0.2. It was therefore more useful for ruling out than ruling in CAP.

Several clinical decision rules have been prospectively validated to help diagnose pneumonia. The simplest rule uses three items (fever, cough, crackles) to stratify the risk of pneumonia. The risk increases from 4% to 11%, 22%, and 48% for women with 0 to 3 factors, respectively. Other rules include those of Heckerling and Diehr, although they have not been prospectively validated.

A large European study (GRACE) identified nearly 3000 patients with acute cough in the primary care setting and obtained a chest radiograph in all of them. They developed a simple 7 item clinical decision rule, although it does incorporate c-reactive protein.A smaller risk score with only 3 items utilizing dyspnea, respiration rates > 20/min, and CRP > 20 mg/l found an area under curve of 0.851 for predicting pneumonia.
Another risk score has been developed to diagnose nursing home acquired pneumonia.
The risk of pneumonia in children with acute cough can be estimated using the STARWAVE clinical rule. Several other prediction models exist for children, particularly in the emergency room.

The Infectious Disease Society of America/American Thoracic Society (IDSA/ATS) and British Thoracic Society guidelines recommend using a validated clinical rule such as the Pneumonia Severity Index, the CURB-65 or the simple CRB-65 along with physician judgment, to assist in site-of-care decisions (). Both tools have been prospectively validated, but the CURB-65 is easier for point of care use while the PSI is preferred by the IDSA 2019 guidelines.

The CRB-65 omits BUN and is therefore more useful in primary care settings. It has 4 elements worth one point each and predicts mortality risk with CAP: age 65+ years, new confusion, respiratory rate >20, and BP <90/60. Patients with 0 points are at low risk for death (LR- 0.1), while those with 3 or 4 points are at increased risk (LR+ 5.6).
Clinical rules can also be used to determine the risk of legionella pneumonia and to identify children with cough and fever who are at low risk for pneumonia.
While qSOFA relatively poor sensitivity, a qSOFA score ≥2 is strongly associated with increased mortality in patients with pneumonia.

Perform a CXR in any patient with acute RTI and at least one of the following abnormal vital signs: temperature higher than 100°F/37.8°C, heart rate greater than 100 bpm, respiratory rate greater than 20 breaths/min; and in any patient with at least two of the following clinical findings: decreased breath sounds, crackles/rales, and absence of asthma).
Obtain a pulse oximetry test, and use the CURB-65, CRB-65, or Pneumonia Severity Index to determine the best site of care (outpatient or inpatient).

For those requiring inpatient care, obtain a sputum and blood culture in patients with severe disease and those being treated empirically for MRSA and P. aeruginosa. Additional diagnostic tests include urinary antigen tests for legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae for patients with severe pneumonia, and thoracentesis for pleural effusion.
The Pneumonia Severity Index, CRB-65, and CURB-65 are validated prognostic models that may be used to help determine site of treatment in patients with CAP (). A
Administer antibiotic therapy as soon as possible after the diagnosis is made and before leaving the ED if the person is being admitted.C

See for detailed recommendations regarding antibiotic choice. Treat previously healthy outpatients with amoxicillin, doxycycline, or (if resistance <25%) a macrolide. For outpatients with comorbidities use (amoxiclav or a cephalosporin) plus (macrolide or doxycycline), OR a respiratory fluoroquinolone.A

For inpatients with nonsevere CAP and no risk factors for MRSA or P. aeruginosa, use combination therapy with a beta-lactam plus a macrolide or doxycycline, OR monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone. For inpatients with severe CAP and no risk factors for MRSA or P. aeruginosa, use a beta-lactam plus macrolide OR beta-lactam plus respiratory fluroquinolone.A
For hospitalized patients with severe CAP, give a systemic corticosteroid which has been shown to reduce mortality, complications, and length of stay.A
Treatment should last at least 5 days and should not be discontinued until the patient has been afebrile for 48 to 72 hours. If stable at 5 days and aferile the antibiotics may be discontinued. A

Administer antibiotic therapy as soon as possible after the diagnosis is made and before leaving the ED if the person is being admitted. Patients should be changed to oral antibiotics once hemodynamically stable and they can take oral medications. This was confirmed by a study that randomized adults with CAP to 5 days of antibiotics and discontinuation if patients are afebrile for 48 hours and otherwise have no signs of hemodynamic instability, or usual care. The median duration of antibiotics in the two groups was 5 vs 10 days. There was no difference in any symptom severity, clinical cure rates, or harms, although the usual care group had a higher 30 day readmission rate (6.6% vs 1.4%, p = 0.02).
Refer to for treatment recommendations consistent with IDSA 2019 guidelines for management of CAP.

The 2019 IDSA guidelines recommend not routinely adding anaerobic coverage for suspected aspiration. Treatment should last at least 5 days and should not be discontinued until the patient has been afebrile for 48 to 72 hours. Treatment longer than 5 days in a patient who is clinically stable is not recommended.
The 2025 update to ATS/IDSA guidelines recommends considering antibiotics for hospitalized patients with CAP even if they have a positive test for a viral pathogen.

A network meta-analysis identified 24 randomized trials comparing different initial oral antibiotics for treatment of CAP. Levofloxacin and nemonoxacin were most likely to provide a clinical response at 2 weeks, while penicillin and amoxicillin were least likely. For the outcome of mortality, levofloxacin, nemonoxacin and azithromycin were most likely to reduce mortality. However, confidence intervals were broad so the confidence in these conclusions is low. Only a single study since 2000 (with 64 patients) studied doxycycline.

A British observational study of hospitalized patients with CAP concluded that the combination of a macrolide (commonly clarithromycin) with a beta-lactam (commonly amoxicillin ± clavulanic acid) was associated with improved 30-day mortality rates in patients with moderate or severe pneumonia, compared to a beta-lactam alone. Mortality rates in the moderate severity group was 22 vs 30% and the severe pneumonia group 45% vs 51%.

Similarly, a non-blinded RCT compared monotherapy with a beta-lactam with a beta-lactam + macrolide in 580 hospitalized immunocompetent adults with CAP. They found that those given combination therapy were more likely to achieve clinical stability at 7 days (NNT = 14) and were less likely to be readmitted within 30 days (NNT = 20).

A meta-analysis of 23 studies comparing a respiratory fluoroquinolone with the combination of a macrolide and a beta-lactam found no difference in effectiveness. Another systematic review of 17 observational studies and 3 RCTs concluded that for adults hospitalized with CAP, a beta-lactam plus a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone were both effective, and should be initiated within 4 to 8 hours of hospital arrival.

There is some concern regarding an increased risk of sudden cardiovascular death among patients using macrolides. A large observational study found that overall, there was a net benefit to adding an azithromycin for elderly patients hospitalized with pneumonia compared with regimens that did not include a macrolide. The NNT was 21 for adding azithromycin to prevent one death, although they also see a number needed to harm of 144 to cause 1 additional MI among patients given azithromycin.

The risk of mycoplasma pneumonia varies greatly between studies, but in general appears to be between 3% and 25% (mean 12%) among patients presenting as outpatients with acute LRTI. A meta-analysis found 5 RCTs with 1912 children diagnosed with mycoplasma pneumonia, but not evidence to support or refute the benefit of antibiotic treatment. A Cochrane review of seven trials with 1912 children reached a similar conclusion.
A randomized trial of 774 adults admitted for CAP (but not to the ICU) compared omadacycline (an aminomethylcycline) to moxafloxacin and found that the new, much more expensive drug was non-inferior.
In a randomized trial of 738 hospitalized patients with CAP, the pleuromutilin antibiotic lefamulin was non-inferior to moxifloxacin. Adverse GI events were more common with lefamulin.

Based on updated IDSA/ATS guidelines (2025) treatment should last at least 3 to 4 days and should not be discontinued until the patient has been clinically improved and stable. Treatment longer than 4 days in a patient who is clinically stable is not recommended.

A systematic review of studies comparing short (≤ 6 days) with longer (> 7 days) duration of antibiotics for CAP found no difference regarding the outcomes of clinical cure using the same antibiotic (5 studies, 1600 patients, RR 1.0, 95% CI 0.97-1.02) or comparing different durations of different antibiotics (13 studies, 1695 patients, RR 1.0, 95% CI 0.96-1.04). Mortality was actually lower with the shorter course in 7 studies with 2028 patients (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.35 - 0.90) and serious adverse events were less likely.
A cohort study identified that excessive treatment with antibiotics was associated with a greater number of patient-reported adverse events and did not improved mortality or readmission rates.

An RCT of 302 patients with severe pneumonia ( Pneumonia Severity Index 110 or higher) found that most patients (if clinically stable, with drop in temperature and able to take oral medications) could be switched safely to an oral antibiotic after 3 days and could leave the hospital an average of 2 days sooner. A second study by the same researchers of 119 adults admitted to the hospital with mild-moderate CAP (Pneumonia Severity Index <110) found that if at 3 days patients had a temperature lower than 38°C, could take oral drugs, and had shown an improvement in symptoms they did just as well taking a placebo as taking an additional 5 days of amoxicillin. If replicated, these findings could guide care of patients with mild pneumonia who are rapidly improving.

A registry found that patients are often prescribed longer than recommended duration of therapy for CAP, with the prescription of an additional 5 to 10 days at discharge commonly the culprit. Those with longer stays and who didn't have antibiotic duration explicitly mentioned in the discharge summary were more likely to receive too long a duration of therapy.
This 2023 meta-analysis advocates for shorter courses of antibiotics in children stating there probably isn't a substantial difference in patient outcomes based on the duration of treatment.

In low-resource health settings, 3 days of amoxicillin was effective in children ages 2-59 months with pneumonia and tachypnea (NNT 43). The study compared amoxicillin vs placebo and the placebo group also had a low treatment failure rate of 4.3%. Another RCT in Malawian children found 3 days of amoxicillin to be inferior to 5 days for treatment of chest-indrawing pneumonia.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of pediatric patients with non-severe CAP found a 3-day course of azithromycin to be noninferior to a 5-day course in terms of treatment failure and had lower rates of gastroenteritis.

An updated guideline from a panel of experts convened by the Society of Critical Care Medicine strongly recommends the administration of steroids for adult patients who are hospitalized with severe CAP. Conditional recommendations also suggest the use of steroids for hospitalized adults with septic shock or ARDS. This is also the recommendation of the updated ATS/IDSA guidelines.

The use of corticosteroids in patients hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia (severe and non-severe) has been associated with reduced time to clinical cure, fewer clinical failures, shorter overall hospital stays, fewer ICU stays, and reduced rates of pneumonia complications.It also as been shown to reduce the likelihood of requiring mechanical ventilation in hospitalized CAP patients, but may increase risk of hospital readmission.

A 2023 RCT randomized 792 patients in the ICU with severe CAP to IV hydrocortisone 200 mg for 4 days or 7 days, depending on the judgment of the medical team, followed by a taper for a total of 8 days or 14 days. All-cause mortality was significantly lower in the hydrocortisone group at 28 days (6.1% vs 11.9%; 95% CI for difference -9.6 to -1.7; NNT = 17) and at 90 days (9.3% vs 14.7%; 95% CI for difference -9.9 to -0.8; NNT = 18). Among patients who did not require mechanical ventilation at enrollment, fewer patients in the treatment group later required it (18.0% vs 29.5%; hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.40 - 0.86; NNT = 9).

A mortality benefit has generally only been seen in patients with severe CAP. In a meta-analysis of RCTs, 12% of the placebo-treated patients with CAP died in the hospital compared to 6% of the corticosteroid-treated patients (NNT=16; 95% CI 10-62). However, a systemic review and meta-analysis looking at all hospitalized adults with CAP did not see a mortality benefit.

An updated systematic review of 15 studies (n=2445) with severe pneumonia and 5 studies (n=1014) of patients with ARDS found reduced mortality in both groups (RR 0.73 for severe CAP, RR 0.77 for ARDS).
A 2023 systemic review (18 studies, 4661 patients) suggests a 7 day course of 6 mg of dexamethasone daily may be the optimal dose. Doses higher than this did not lead to any mortality benefit.

In patients with low risk (i.e. non-severe) community-acquired pneumonia, a nonblinded RCT demonstrated that the implementation of early mobilization, nutrition screening, early switch from IV to oral antibiotics, and adjunctive treatment with corticosteroids, did not affect length of stay, mortality, readmission rate, or need for intensive care support in hospitalized patients, but had higher rates of gastrointestinal bleeding likely secondary to the steroids.

A trial in Kenya found a reduction in 30-day mortality was less likely in the steroid group (22.6% vs 26.0%; P = .02; number needed to treat [NNT] = 29). However, the overall mortality rate of 24% in this study was actually higher than that for studies of patients with severe CAP in the United States and Europe. Therefore, these results must be cautiously extrapolated to high-resource settings because of a lack of diagnostic confirmation, high rates of comorbid HIV infection (30%), and a lack of access to ICUs in low-resource settings.

According to a meta-analysis of RCTs, the mortality benefit from corticosteroid treatment was not seen in children but it did reduce the likelihood of clinical failure and decreased the time to clinical cure.

For the treatment of refractory Mycoplasma pneumoniae, corticosteroids can improve the clinical outcomes in pediatric patients. However, the authors of the systematic review and meta-analysis stated the evidence is limited due to the quality and quantity of the included literature.

Immunocompromised patients include those with primary immunodeficiencies, undergoing active chemotherapy, chronic corticosteroids, post-transplant, persons with HIV and CD4 count < 200 cells/mcl, and persons receiving biologics and disease-modifyhing antirheumatic drugs.

In addition to the usual pathogens seen in non-immunocompromised persons, bacteria seen in the immunocompromised include enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonoas, acinetobacter, MRSA, nocardia species, mycobacteria, and rhodococcus equi. Viruses include cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and varicilla zoster. Fungi include pneumocystis jirovecii, aspergillus, mucorales species, histoplasma, cryptococcus, blastomyces, and coccidiodes species. Parasites include toxoplasma gondii and strongyloides stercoralis.

Initial antibiotic selection may warrant more extended range antibiotics, targetting specific risk factors such as previous colonization or infection. A consensus statement (2020) addresses evaluation and therapy in immunocompromised patients with community-acquired pneumonia.
Vitamin C may have a role in the prevention or treatment of pneumonia, but the evidence is still preliminary.
Vitamin A has been studied in the pediatric population, but no benefit has been documented for CAP in adults.

Early mobilization is important. In a study of 458 patients with CAP admitted to 17 hospitals, those randomized to early mobilization (encouraged to get into upright position for at least 20 minutes during the first 24 hours and progressively more after that) went home much sooner (5.8 vs 6.9 days, 95% CI, 0–2.2).
Based on limited evidence (six small RCTs), chest physiotherapy was not found to be useful as an adjunct in patients with pneumonia.
There is no evidence of benefit for over-the-counter medications for cough associated with CAP.
Provide oxygen as needed to prevent hypoxemia.
No evidence exists to support routine use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor in adults with pneumonia.

Treatment should last at least 5 days and should not be discontinued until the patient has been afebrile for 48 to 72 hours. Treatment longer than 5 days in a patient who is clinically stable is not recommended.
Use validated measures (Pneumonia Severity Index and CURB-65) to aid in the decision to admit (see Clinical Decision Rules section and ).
Admit patients with septic shock or acute respiratory failure to the ICU.

Cases of pneumonia that should be reported to the state or local health department include legionnaires’ disease, psittacosis, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), suspected terrorist agents (eg, plague, tularemia, or anthrax), and those cases not endemic to the area or those thought to be part of a cluster or outbreak.
Nonresponse or treatment failure occurs in 6% to 15% of hospitalized patients.

Further diagnostic testing is usually necessary and may include repeat or initial serum and sputum microbiologic testing, urinary tests for legionella and S. pneumoniae antigens, chest CT, thoracentesis, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL).
Consider CAP patients with persistent shock despite adequate fluid resuscitation for drotrecogin alpha-activated therapy within 24 hours of admission.
Evaluate patients with CAP and persistent hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation for occult adrenal insufficiency.

Switch patients from IV to oral therapy when they are stable and improving clinically. An RCT of 302 patients with severe pneumonia found that most patients (if clinically stable, with drop in temperature, and able to take oral medications) could be switched safely to an oral antibiotic after 3 days and could leave the hospital an average of 2 days sooner.

Another comparing guideline directed care (5 days with discontinuation if clinically stable) with usual care (average duration of antibiotics 10 days) found no difference in outcomes, and a higher readmission rate in the usual care group.
There is no need for inpatient observation of patients on oral therapy.

Discuss smoking cessation with all smokers admitted for CAP. Assess all patients for vaccine status upon treatment for CAP, and administer vaccines during outpatient treatment or at hospital discharge, if necessary and available.
A Cochrane review concluded based on a review of 22 trials with 2372 patients that febrile neutropenic cancer patients who were hemodyamically stable, oral antibiotics were an acceptable option.
The Pneumonia Severity Index,, CURB-65, and CRB-65 (no labs required) are useful prognostic tools that can assist physicians in evaluating disease severity (). A
For outpatients younger than 65 years, improvement is expected within 48 to 72 hours with work return in 4 to 5 days and full improvement by 2 weeks. C

Overall mortality is 0.6% for outpatients and 8% for inpatients. Most deaths (70%) are due to complications such as respiratory failure, congestive heart failure, shock, dysrhythmia, myocardial infarction, GI bleed, or renal insufficiency.
For outpatients younger than 65 years, improvement is expected within 48 to 72 hours, with work return in 4 to 5 days and full improvement by 2 weeks.
Clinical stability is expected within 3 to 7 days for inpatients.

The Severe Community Acquired Pneumonia (SCAP) is a new predictive score consisting of eight variables (arterial pH <7.30; systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg; respiratory rate >30/min; altered mental status; blood urea nitrogen >30 mg/dL; oxygen arterial pressure <54 mm Hg or ratio of arterial oxygen tension to fraction of inspired oxygen <250 mm Hg; age 80 years; and multilobar/bilateral lung affectation) summed for a total score; low risk is a score of 0 to 1. The SCAP may perform better than the PSI and CURB-65 in predicting patients with CAP at low risk of death as a higher percentage of patients were accurately classified as low risk.

Predictors of 30 day readmission include poor nurse-patient communications, iatrogenic pneumothorax, and poor staff responsiveness to patient needs. Higher RN staffing was associated with decreased readmission rates.

The Yale New Haven Readmission Risk Score (YNHRRS) for pneumonia is a clinical tool that can aid in the assessment of 30-day readmission risk. This model uses a weighted anaylsis of 25 predictor variables including age, sex, nursing home resident status, commorbidities, vital signs, and key laboratory and imaging findings.

In hospitalized patients with CAP, qSOFA in combination with admission lactate was the best predictor of 28-day mortality in a study comparing several clinical prediction rules ( CURB65, PSI, SOFA, qSOFA, and admission lactate) in predicting mortality.
The ration of lactate dehydrogenase to albumin is a predictor of mortality in patients hospitalized with lower RTI, with an AUC of 081.

The British Thoracic Society guidelines recommend a follow-up CXR for patients with persistent signs and symptoms or for those who are at higher risk of underlying malignancy (eg, smokers and those 50 years or older).2019 ATS/IDSA guidelines do not recommend routine follow up chest imaging. The rate of repeat imaging detecting a new malignancy varies from 0.2-5%. However, most of these patients meet the criteria for lung cancer screening and should proceed with the screening CT scans.
In a group of elderly patients with pneumonia, rates of CXR resolution were 35% at 3 weeks, 58% at 6 weeks, 68% at 9 weeks, and 76% at 12 weeks.
Fever is frequently absent in older patients.
A respiratory rate greater than 24 breaths/min is the most sensitive sign of pneumonia in the elderly.
Influenza vaccine is recommended for women who will be pregnant during the flu season.
There is insufficient evidence from three studies with 280 patients to determine whether pneumococcal vaccination during pregnancy reduces infant infections.

feature.caption: Treatment of Community-Acquired Pneumonia (2019 IDSA guidelines).

tr.td: Outpatient with no comorbidities or risk factors for MRSA or pseudomonas
Amoxicillin, doxycycline or (if <25% hmacrolide resistance locally) a macrolide.
Outpatient with comorbidities (chronic heart, lung, liver, or renal disease; diabetes mellitus; alcoholism; malignancy; or asplenia)

1. Amoxicillin/clavulanate or cephalosporin (Cefopodoxime 200 mg bid or cefuroxime 500 mg bid) AND macrolide or doxycycline OR2. Monotherapy with respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg daily, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily, or gemifloxacin 320 mg daily)
Inpatients with non-severe CAP and no risk factors for MRSA or pseudomonas

Beta-lactam (ampicillin 1 sulbactam 1.5–3 g every 6 h, cefotaxime 1–2 g every 8 h, ceftriaxone 1–2 g daily, or ceftaroline 600 mg every 12 h) and a macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg daily or clarithromycin 500 mg bid) ORRespiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily)
Macrolide + beta-lactam OR respiratory fluoroquinolone + beta-lactam
For inpatients with risk factors for MRSA, add coverage at right
Vancomycin (15 mg/kg every 12 hours, adjust based on levels) or linezolid (600 mg q 12 hours)
Inpatient with risk factors for pseudomonas, add coverage as shown at right
Piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g every 6 h), cefepime (2 g every 8 h), ceftazidime (2 g every 8 h), aztreonam (2 g every 8 h), meropenem (1 g every 8 h), or imipenem (500 mg every 6 h)
Oseltamivir or zanamivir but only if within 48 hours of symptoms
